# Yarrek

*Goat Herder*

## Personality

Gentle, slow to speak and devoted to his goats, each of which he knows by name.

## Lore

Yarrek leads the Tolmach goats between the high pastures and the camps, and he knows every one of them by name. He is forty-seven, gentle and slow to speak, and he can go a whole morning on the slopes without saying a word to a person while saying a great many quiet things to goats. The Tolmach say that if a goat ever learned to talk, it would talk like Yarrek: rarely, kindly, and only about the weather and the grass.

### On the paths

Yarrek was born in a hide tent in the Tolmach camps, the son of a herding family that has walked the same seasonal paths for longer than anyone can count. His parents are both long dead; his father taught him the herd, and his mother taught him to sing to it, which he still does under his breath on the steep stretches. He has never wanted any other work. When the herds go up to the high pastures in spring and down toward the valleys in autumn, Yarrek walks at the back, where the stragglers are, because that is where a herder learns the most.

He married Harra fifteen years ago. She is shrewd, cheerful and loud enough to be heard across the whole Trading Post, where she sells the herds' wool, hides and cheese and drives famously hard bargains with lowland traders. Everyone in the camps thought the match was a joke at first, the loudest woman in the family and its quietest man. They have been proved wrong for fifteen years. Harra talks for both of them, Yarrek listens for both of them, and each thinks the other got the better bargain. Harra's mother, Mabbu, approves of him in her own way, which is to scold him and feed him in the same breath.

### Kesh

Their son Kesh is nine and has, his parents agree, inherited all of the talking and none of the quiet. Yarrek has trusted him with the kids of the herd since last year, and taught him to name every one, as his own father taught him. Kesh's names run to Grumble, Biter and Lady Snort, and Yarrek treats each with perfect seriousness. He is not yet ready to give the boy the grown goats, and he has explained why so gently that Kesh still thinks it unfair.

### The neighbour at the cisterns

The Tolmach camps nearest town draw water from the same terrace cisterns as the Kragvar, and Yarrek's family shares its tanks with Gorra, the cistern keeper. Their arrangement is fair to the bucket and argued over weekly, Gorra counting and Yarrek nodding, and neither would give it up for anything. It was under one of Gorra's cistern lids that Kesh and her son Korrin first met, hiding from the pair of them.

### The three goats

This year Sennu, the Tolmach chieftain, has kept the herds closer to town than ever because of the monsters in the low valleys. But goats stray. Last month three of Yarrek's goats slipped away in the night and were found two days later, coming back up from the valley on their own. They were wild-eyed and biting, and they have not been right since. They will not eat from his hand. They butt the fence and stare at nothing. Yarrek keeps them penned apart from the herd, and every evening he sits beside their pen and talks to them softly, the way he talks to all his goats, hoping they will calm.

He does not know what happened to them in the valley. He has described them to anyone who will listen, which for Yarrek is a great deal of talking, and he has noticed that Ahvi the song-keeper listened harder than anyone, and then went very quiet.

### Hopes and fears

Yarrek wants his three goats back as they were. He fears they will not come back, and he fears, more quietly, that they will not be the last. He has started counting the herd twice each evening, as the chieftain does.

A quest could follow the goats' tracks down into the valley to find what they met there, or help Yarrek bring a calming herb up from the far slopes.
